extracted.intended_audience: high-school student journalists, copy readers, and proofreaders
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for copy reading, proofreading, head-line writing, hyphenation, and story-leading specifically aimed at school (especially high-school) newspaper production. Covers punctuation, compound-word conventions, proofreader marks, headline composition rules, and how to lead different story types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe for possessive singular
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ’s to form the possessive singular of a noun: John’s book, the ship’s rudder, Burns’s poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that some authorities drop the final s with names ending in s (Burns’ poems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Apostrophe for plurals of letters and numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an apostrophe + s to form plurals of letters and numbers: He made his Q’s and 2’s exactly alike.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use an apostrophe before the final s in possessive adjectives (hers, its, ours, theirs, yours). Example: It's (contraction) vs its (possessive): It’s hard to find its equal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound adjectives preceding a noun take a hyphen
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound adjectives or common nouns used adjectively take the hyphen, e.g., first-class man, two-story house, apple-pie order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: phrases like one- or two-story house may be treated without hyphen in some constructions (the text notes 'one or two story house, etc., do not take the hyphen').

rubrics_metrics.name: No hyphen with adverbs ending in -ly + participle
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverbs ending in -ly compounded with participles do not take the hyphen, as in 'a newly built house'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not hyphenate adverb+past-participle combinations when the adverb ends in -ly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compounds with self/ante/post/semi/anti prefixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound words with the prefixes self, ante, post, semi, and anti take the hyphen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples implied by rule; apply hyphen with these specific prefixes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make one word with certain prefixes (re, non, over, under, sub, inter, trans)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words formed by prefixing re, non, over, under, sub, and similar prefixes make one word; inter- and trans- combinations are also united as prefixes (interstate, interscholastic, intercollegiate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such prefixed forms as solid (no hyphen, no space).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffix -like written as one word; hyphenate when triple letters occur
rubrics_metrics.description: Like used as a suffix is written as one word: childlike, manlike, sphinalike. If three l’s come together, use the hyphen: bell-like, ball-like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write -like as one word except hyphenate to avoid awkward triple letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefix+specific nouns syllable rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When words such as man, men, yard, maker, tender, keeper, seeker, holder, master, owner, house, and room are given prefixes of one syllable, the combination is written as one word; when the prefix is two or more syllables, the combination is written as two words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this syllable-count rule to decide solid vs. separate form (guidance illustrated by many examples in the list).

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain combinations are written as one solid word (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: A long list of commonly solid compound words that should be written as one word (airship, bankbook, birdseye, breechloader, bylaws, catchpenny, committeeman, crowbar, downstairs, eyewitness, figurehead, goodbye, hardwood, hairpin, housebuilder, lightweight, nearsighted, paperhanger, powwow, rainstorm, schoolhouse, smallpox, today, warehouseman, wrongdoing, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these listed combinations as single words; the list functions as authoritative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certain combinations are written as separate words (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some combinations should be written as separate words: any one, a while, bucket shop, en route, back yard, front yard, live stock, lodging house, custom house, plate glass, street car, tide water, vice president, water works, White House, right of way, commander in chief, editor in chief, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided list as authoritative guidance for separate-word forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific combinations require a hyphen (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some expressions should be hyphenated: anti-trust, a-hunting, bric-a-brae, brother-in-law, mud-slinging, poet-painter, secretary-treasurer, semi-finals, so-called, king, ship-rigged, 6-year-old child, tête-à-tête, two-thirds, two-story house, un-American, un-Christian, well-known man, world-weary, work-worn, co-ed (slang).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the list for hyphenation; numerical-age compounds (6-year-old) and multiword kinship terms are examples to hyphenate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strike-out and correction method
rubrics_metrics.description: If the copy reader desires to strike out a word or a line, he should draw a mark through it; never enclose it in parentheses, and never attempt to erase it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear strike-throughs rather than erasures or parentheses to avoid confusion for the compositor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate numbers/figures clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Circle a number you wish spelled out or circle a spelled-out number you wish set in figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: indicate whether 'seventy-five' should be set as '75' by circling appropriately; use these marks consistently so typesetters know preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition and movement marks
rubrics_metrics.description: When words, letters, or sentences need to be transposed, the copy reader should indicate the necessary change with transposition marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard transposition/proof-reader marks (examples shown in the proof marks list) rather than writing editorial notes in body text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mark paragraph beginnings and ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark the beginning of every paragraph with the paragraph mark and place an end mark at the conclusion of every story to indicate nothing is to be added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent paragraph and end marking prevents compositors from running paragraphs together or adding stray copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate run-together words with a diagonal
rubrics_metrics.description: If words have been run together improperly, separate them by a diagonal mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: anypne → any/pone (mark shows intended separation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Print all names and clarify ambiguous letters
rubrics_metrics.description: In longhand copy print all names; underscore certain letters and overscore others to avoid misreading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text advises special marking (underscore w’s and w’s, overscore n’s and m’s — follow local conventions) to ensure compositors can decipher handwritten letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stet and folio copy conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: If you wish words to stand which you have struck out, make a row of dots under them and mark 'stet' in the margin; write 'folio copy' in the margin when you wish copy containing misspellings or bad grammar set as written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'stet' to restore struck text and a clear marginal note (folio copy) to indicate copy must be set exactly as submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking for type emphasis (italics, small caps, capitals, bold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Underscore a word once for italics, twice for SMALL CAPITALS, and three times for CAPITALS. To indicate bold-face, mark 'B. F.' in the margin beside the part to be set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the underscore-count convention consistently; use 'B. F.' for boldface and write other formatting instructions clearly in margins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide compositor instructions for measure/columns
rubrics_metrics.description: If a piece of copy is to be set in double column or in narrow measure, write the necessary instructions for the compositor in the margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include layout instructions (double column, narrow measure) clearly in the margin to avoid typesetting errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make only necessary corrections and write legibly
rubrics_metrics.description: Make no corrections that are not absolutely necessary and write all corrections as neatly and legibly as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unnecessary or messy corrections lead to typesetting errors and extra charges; legibility saves time and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strike out every word not to be printed
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful to strike out every word on the copy that you do not wish printed, for every word that is not struck out will be set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to strike unwanted words results in them being printed; double-check omissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare manuscripts to minimize typesetting/correction charges
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the copy so clear and legible that the compositor will be able to read it at a glance; by care in preparing manuscripts the copy reader can save extra charges for typesetting and corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neat, well-marked copy saves money and reduces errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline primary purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: A headline has two purposes: first, to attract attention, and second, to tell the story. If it succeeds in both it is excellent; if only one, mediocre; if neither, useless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a headline can do only one thing well, it is better that it attract attention without telling the story than that it tell the story without attracting attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline should contain the feature of the story
rubrics_metrics.description: The headline should contain the feature of the story unless the story is written in suspense order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the story's main feature as the headline lead unless suspense structure requires otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline should contain a verb (expressed or implied)
rubrics_metrics.description: The headline should contain a verb, either expressed or implied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example style: 'ROCKEFELLER GIVES OIL KING GENEROUS DIMES TO URCHINS WITH SHINY DIMES' — headlines without verbs feel weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beginning multi-line headlines with an implied-subject verb
rubrics_metrics.description: The headline of more than a single one-line bank should never begin with a verb of which the subject is to be understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on the reader to supply the subject when a headline spans multiple lines; structure so each bank makes sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer active verbs in headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: An active verb is stronger in a headline than a passive verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show active phrasing is punchier: 'Boy of 10 Captures Desperate Outlaw' is stronger than 'Outlaw Is Captured by Boy'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headlines must 'break on sense' (no awkward line breaks)
rubrics_metrics.description: The parts of a prepositional phrase or an infinitive should never be separated at the end of a line in a dropline heading; the line should 'break on sense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrate better vs. worse line breaks; avoid splitting cohesive phrases across lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit unnecessary articles and words from headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: The headline should never contain one of the articles a, an, the, or any other unnecessary word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep headlines tight — drop filler words that do not add information or punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not abbreviate words in headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: No word should be abbreviated in a headline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out words fully for clarity and professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not repeat important words in a headline
rubrics_metrics.description: No important word should be used twice in a headline, even if the headline is composed of several banks; use a synonym if repetition would occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: avoid repeating the same noun across banks; choose a synonym to vary wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each bank of a multi-bank heading must add information and connect
rubrics_metrics.description: Every bank in a 'top' heading should add something to the information preceding banks have presented, and every bank should have some evident connection with the banks that precede and follow it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each line of a multi-line headline should progress the information rather than repeat or stray.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count letters and spaces so headline fits allotted space
rubrics_metrics.description: Since type cannot be stretched or compressed, the copy reader must count the letters and spaces in banks of headings set in capital letters and the words in banks set in capitals and lower case; never write a line which exceeds the number of units that can be set or which does not contain enough units to fill the space properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write headlines that will physically look well in type; avoid lines too long or too short for the column.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand-set headline and slugging procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Headlines which are to be set by hand must be written on separate sheets of paper, and the stories which they are to surmount must be 'slugged' with the first two words of the top banks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the mechanical workflow for hand-set type: separate headline sheets and slugs to help compositors match headline to story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linotype headline placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every headline which is to be set on the linotype machine must be written at the beginning of the story it is to surmount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place linotype headlines at the head of the copy to assist linotype operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number headlines according to head schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: Every headline must be marked plainly with its proper number according to the head schedule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the publication's head schedule numbering system for consistency in layout and composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid weak slang, forced humor, rhyme, alliteration, and puns in headlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Weak slang and forced humor are best omitted from headlines; rhyme, alliteration, and puns are poor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep headlines direct and professional; novelty devices are usually inferior to clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headlines must be accurate and avoid overstating facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The headline must be accurate. It must never overstate the facts for the sake of effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy trumps sensationalism in headline writing; do not mislead readers for impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: If story lacks sufficient news for headline, reconsider printing
rubrics_metrics.description: If a story does not contain enough interesting news to make a headline, the probability is that it does not merit printing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider newsworthiness before allocating headline space; weak stories often should be spiked or rewritten.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three common story types for school papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Most stories for high school papers fall into three groups: (1) reports of interviews, speeches, and meetings; (2) accounts of athletic games and contests; and (3) descriptions of social events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that feature articles, 'follow' stories, and rewrites are less common in school papers; choose treatment appropriate to the type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview-story lead options
rubrics_metrics.description: In the lead of a news story of a personal interview the reporter may feature: (1) the name of the person interviewed, (2) a direct quotation, (3) an indirect quotation, (4) the subject discussed, (5) the reason for the interview, (6) the occasion, or (7) the place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the most newsworthy of these seven points for the lead; emphasize local interest and prefer a striking quotation over simply naming the subject if it improves interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech-story lead guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead to an account of a speech or lecture may feature: (1) the theme or title, (2) a direct quotation, (3) an indirect quotation, (4) the name of the speaker, (5) the purpose of the speech, (6) the occasion, or (7) the place or time of delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dullness by noting only important points; readers likely heard the speech and do not need a detailed blow-by-blow review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report-of-meetings lead options
rubrics_metrics.description: Points which may be featured in the lead to an account of a meeting are: (1) the purpose of the meeting, (2) the names of the groups or organizations taking part, (3) the important business transacted, (4) the names of speakers or entertainers, (5) the special entertainment offered, (6) the occasion, or (7) rarely the place or time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize the meeting's purpose and important actions; include speakers and significant items of business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports lead rule: 'When in doubt, play the score.'
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead of a sport story may always feature the result of a game or contest ('play the score').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other lead options include spectacular plays, work of individual players, names/records of teams, significance of outcome, equality/inequality of opponents, conditions affecting results, spectator numbers/actions, and time/place of contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sports vernacular appropriately; avoid vulgar or meaningless slang
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter should use sport vernacular in writing the story of a game, but should try to avoid vulgar and meaningless slang.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn and use commonly accepted sporting terms; avoid inventing extravagant expressions — useful slang will survive, useless coinages will not.
